To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in silico deployment of the Parachute device reduced myofiber stress by 61.2% in the lower chamber and that adjusting material properties to simulate the 6-month CT data resulted in further reductions in stress (27.1% in the upper chamber and 78.4% in the lower).
the Parachute® reduced the myofiber stress by 27% in the upper chamber and 78% in the lower chamber at end-diastolic, and by 10% in the upper and 8% in the lower at end-systolic.

the finite element model of the Parachute® was associated with reduced myofiber stress in the lower chamber and that a model with altered material parameters was associated with reduced diastolic stiffness, reduced myofiber stresses at the upper and lower chambers, and unchanged stroke volume.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and applying computational models to understand the biomechanical and hemodynamic effects of the Parachute®.
the development of a computational model of the Parachute device and its effects on left ventricle function.
developing and validating a computational model of LV mechanics that is capable of simulating the effects of the Parachute®.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Parachute® may be effective for reversing LV remodeling and restoring normal pump function.
the Parachute® appears to have a beneficial effect on LV function and geometry.
this study suggests that the primary mechanism for the Parachute® to reduce myofiber stress is through a reduction in LV diastole stiffness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Parachute® appears to reduce myofiber stress in the lower chamber and to reduce the stiffness of the LV wall.
the Parachute® may reverse post-infarct left ventricular remodeling through a decrease in end-diastolic myofiber stress.
we developed a patient specific model of the Parachute® that is able to simulate the acute and chronic effects of the device.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patient-specific modeling is an efficient means to study the mechanical effects of novel devices.
patient-specific finite element modeling can be used to assess the mechanical effects of a new cardiac device and to guide its design and optimization.
the Parachute® may be a viable option for the treatment of patients with post-infarct heart failure, but further study is required.
